content.title: ACT Writing: Constructing Introduction, Body, and Conclusion
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the structural alignment of an ACT essay. It teaches the 'One-Sentence Purpose Map' strategy to ensure the introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion work together to support a single, clear claim.
learning_objectives: Draft a clear introduction sentence that establishes a claim and an essay angle.
Construct body paragraph link sentences that connect evidence and reasons back to the central claim.
Formulate a conclusion that restates the claim and explains its broader significance.

sections.title: The One-Sentence Purpose Map
sections.content: The One-Sentence Purpose Map is a structural strategy used to ensure an essay remains focused and organized. It involves drafting three specific types of sentences: an Intro Purpose Sentence, Body Link Sentences, and a Concluding Restatement. By aligning these three elements before or during the drafting process, you ensure that every part of the essay serves the central argument. This prevents the common issue of 'drifting' where body paragraphs or conclusions lose sight of the original thesis.

sections.title: The Introduction: Claim and Angle
sections.content: A strong introduction must do more than just state a topic; it must establish a claim (your position) and an angle (the specific scope or perspective you will take). The Intro Purpose Sentence should be a concise statement that tells the reader exactly what you are arguing and how you intend to approach the issue.

sections.title: The Body: Linking Evidence to Claim
sections.content: Each body paragraph should be anchored by a 'link sentence.' This sentence performs three functions: it identifies a supporting reason, references specific evidence, and explicitly connects both back to the main claim. This ensures that the paragraph is not just a list of facts, but a functional part of the overall argument.

sections.title: The Conclusion: Restatement and Context
sections.content: The conclusion should not merely repeat the introduction. Instead, it should restate the claim in a way that reflects the evidence presented in the body. Furthermore, it should provide a 'broader context'—explaining the wider significance or implications of the claim to show the essay's purpose in a real-world or theoretical setting.

worked_examples.question: Issue: Should high schools implement a four-day school week? Use the One-Sentence Purpose Map to outline a supportive argument.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1 (Intro): Write a claim with an angle. 'High schools should adopt a four-day week to improve student mental health and reduce operational costs.' Step 2 (Body Link): Connect a reason to evidence and the claim. 'By providing a mid-week break, schools can reduce student burnout, which directly supports the goal of improving overall mental health.' Step 3 (Conclusion): Restate the claim with broader significance. 'Transitioning to a four-day schedule not only benefits individual well-being but also creates a more sustainable and modern educational model for the future.'

common_mistakes: Writing a conclusion that introduces entirely new arguments not mentioned in the body.
Failing to link body paragraph evidence back to the central claim, leaving the reader to guess the relevance.
Using a vague introduction that states the topic but fails to take a clear position (claim).
exam_tips: Before writing, mentally check if your intro, body links, and conclusion form a logical sequence.
Ensure your conclusion answers the 'So what?' question by explaining why your claim matters in a larger context.
Use transition words in your body link sentences to show how evidence 'supports,' 'proves,' or 'reinforces' your claim.
content.recap: A well-organized ACT essay uses a clear introduction to set the claim, body paragraphs that explicitly link evidence back to that claim, and a conclusion that restates the position within a broader, meaningful context.

knowledge_claims.content: The One-Sentence Purpose Map involves drafting one sentence for the intro, one link sentence per body paragraph, and one concluding sentence.
An Intro Purpose Sentence must include both the essay's overall claim and its intended angle or scope.
Each body paragraph requires a link sentence that ties a supporting reason and evidence back to the central claim.
A concluding restatement should explain the claim's wider significance or implications rather than just repeating the thesis.
To verify organization, read the intro claim, body links, and conclusion in sequence to see if they form a coherent argument.
It is a mistake to introduce brand new evidence or unrelated arguments in the conclusion.
A body paragraph lacks focus if it lists evidence without a sentence explicitly connecting that evidence to the main claim.
The 'angle' of an introduction defines the specific perspective or boundaries the writer will use to argue their claim.
The 'broader context' in a conclusion answers why the argument matters in a real-world or theoretical sense.
When a draft fragment feels disconnected, the first step is to state the main claim in one clear intro sentence.
Unlike the introduction which sets the scope, the conclusion reflects on the evidence already presented to show the essay's purpose.
A body link sentence must perform three functions: state a reason, reference evidence, and connect to the claim.

items.stem:
ACT WRITING PRACTICE: Automation and Human Judgment

Schools and workplaces increasingly use automated systems to schedule tasks, identify patterns, and recommend decisions. These systems may increase efficiency, but they can also make it harder to see how a decision was reached.

Perspective 1: Automated recommendations should be widely adopted whenever they outperform unaided human judgment.
Perspective 2: Important decisions should remain primarily human because responsibility cannot be delegated to a system.
Perspective 3: Automation is most valuable when it provides evidence that people can inspect, question, and override.

Write a unified, coherent essay in which you evaluate multiple perspectives on the issue and develop your own perspective. Explain the relationship between your perspective and at least one other perspective. Support your ideas with reasoning and examples.
items.correctAnswer: Scored holistically with the four ACT Writing domains
items.explanation: A strong response states a defensible position, engages at least one supplied perspective, develops reasoning and examples, organizes ideas coherently, and controls language and conventions.

items.stem:
ACT WRITING PRACTICE: Water Conservation and Consumer Choice

Regions facing drought can rely on voluntary conservation or impose limits on water use.

Perspective 1: Institutions should adopt the option that produces the greatest measurable efficiency and access.
Perspective 2: Decisions should protect human relationships, local character, and individual judgment even when doing so is less efficient.
Perspective 3: A flexible policy with transparent safeguards can combine the strongest features of both approaches.
